hook_text: The light from the star next to the Southern Cross left it more than four years ago. And it is the closest star there is, after the Sun.
clip_script: Here is a trick question: what is the nearest star? The answer is the Sun, a ball of hot gas making its own light, just eight light minutes away. The next nearest are beside the Southern Cross. The brighter of the two Pointers looks like one golden star, but a telescope shows it is three: Alpha Centauri A and B, two suns circling each other, and a tiny red dwarf called Proxima Centauri, discovered from Johannesburg in 1915. Proxima is 4.24 light years away. That is forty trillion kilometres. Shrink the Sun to a soccer ball in Johannesburg and the nearest star is another soccer ball in Cairo, with almost nothing in between. Our fastest spacecraft would take seventy-five thousand years to get there. So when you look at Alpha Centauri tonight, you are seeing light that left before you started this school year.
visual_style: A whiteboard Southern Cross with two Pointers, a zoom into the brighter Pointer splitting into three labelled stars, then a map of Africa with a soccer ball in Johannesburg and another in Cairo.
pacing: A trick question, a reveal in the sky, then a scale that sticks.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to find Alpha Centauri tonight.
